docs.text:
LightnerX is a modular static C++ library for building applications that communicate using the INER semantic protocol. The CMake project provides the LightnerX target; it neither produces nor requires its own executable. The library provides types for representing messages, interpreters, callbacks, connection management, and a transport layer based on GameNetworkingSockets. INER defines the meaning of messages exchanged between an Authority and an Obedient. It does not define sockets, connections, or an execution model. These capabilities are provided by LightnerX's networking components and can be connected to the application according to the developer's needs. Library, not a framework ¶ LightnerX provides reusable components. The consuming application decides: when to initialize and shut down components; how to run update() ; which threads to use; how to organize the connection lifecycle; which modules to use or replace with its own implementations. For example, you can pass one complete INER message from your own transport to lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter . authorityInterpret does not require a connection. obedientInterpret requires a lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager registration: add() accepts only live GNS handles, so arbitrary identifiers from another transport are not supported by that path. The manager stores its own mapping and does not use GNS connection userdata. Key concepts ¶ Authority: controls internal states and receives intentions from the Obedient. Obedient: sends intentions to the Authority and receives events and responses. Event: an occurrence communicated by the Authority. Response: the result of an intention sent by the Obedient. Intention: an action request sent to the Authority. Notification: information sent to the Authority without requesting a state change. INER message flow ¶ The INER protocol defines four message types exchanged between the Authority and the Obedient: flowchart LR A["🖥️ AUTHORITY
Server"] O["💻 OBEDIENT
Client"] A -->|EVENT| O A -->|RESPONSE| O O -->|INTENTION| A O -->|NOTIFICATION| A classDef authority fill:#123456,stroke:#2699ff,color:#fff,stroke-width:2px classDef obedient fill:#302050,stroke:#a76bee,color:#fff,stroke-width:2px class A authority class O obedient linkStyle 0 stroke:#2596ee,stroke-width:3px linkStyle 1 stroke:#16a085,stroke-width:3px linkStyle 2 stroke:#e69b27,stroke-width:3px linkStyle 3 stroke:#a76bee,stroke-width:3px In LightnerX, the application connects components through callbacks: the network delivers bytes, and MessageInterpreter interprets those bytes according to the direction of communication. When sending, lightnerx::network::Target lets you select a connection, a group, or a broadcast with or without exceptions. Navigation ¶ Setup First steps Communication and the INER protocol API reference Server example ¶ This example receives notifications from the client and sends the text Hello, World! in events to registered connections. The snippets below make up the complete program at the end of the README; the statements belong inside the main function, after the imports shown in the complete code. Create the components ¶ The manager maps handles to internal client IDs. Register ID 47 so that the interpreter recognizes notifications sent by the client in this example. using namespace std::chrono_literals; namespace network = lightnerx::network; namespace communication = lightnerx::communication; network::Server server; network::ConnectionManager connections{30, 30}; communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; communication::NotificationRegistry notifications; notifications.registerId(47); Track connections ¶ The callbacks keep the manager up to date. If registering a connection fails, the server requests its disconnection. server.addClientConnectedCallback([&](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (!connections.add(connection)) { if (const auto result = server.disconnectConnection(connection, false); !result) { std::println("Failed to disconnect: {}", result.error().message()); } } }); server.addClientDisconnectedCallback([&](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (const auto id = connections.getClientId(connection)) { connections.remove(*id); } }); Receive messages ¶ Forward the received bytes to obedientInterpret . The interpreter's callback delivers the message and the internal client ID. In this example, the payload is text and is read during the callback. server.addClientReceivedMessageCallback( [&](std::span bytes, HSteamNetConnection connection) { interpreter.obedientInterpret(bytes, notifications, connection, connections); } ); interpreter.addObedientInterpretedMessageCallback( [](communication::Message message, std::uint16_t clientId) { const std::string_view text{ reinterpret_cast(message.payload.data()), message.payload.size() }; std::println("Client {}: {}", clientId, text); } ); Start the server ¶ Start listening on port 41333 , with an established connection timeout of 3000 ms, and reserve one slot for the batcher's pending message. if (const auto result = server.start(41333, 3000); !result) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", result.error().message()); return 1; } network::initMessagesBatcher(1); Prepare an event ¶ Convert the text to bytes and include the header and payload in the total size. For Event , the size is shifted one bit to the left. Type 990 is chosen by the application. const std::string_view greeting = "Hello, World!"; const auto payload = std::as_bytes(std::span{greeting}); const communication::Event event{ // The least significant bit distinguishes Event from Response. static_cast((sizeof(communication::Event) + payload.size()) << 1), 990 }; Update and send ¶ update() processes the network. The converter creates an OutboundMessage , which is passed directly to queueMessage . Target::broadcast() selects the connections registered at flush time. while (true) { if (const auto result = server.update(); !result) { std::println("Failed to update: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (const auto result = network::queueMessage(communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, network::Target::broadcast())); !result) { std::println("Failed to queue: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (const auto result = network::flushAll(connections); !result) { std::println("Failed to send: {}", result.error().message()); break; } std::this_thread::sleep_for(3s); } queueMessage takes ownership of the message, including when it returns an error; the application does not call Release() afterward. flushAll processes the queue and releases the messages. The three-second interval is a choice made for this example; the application defines its own update rate. Shut down the server ¶ After exiting the loop due to an error, close the server. Returning 1 signals an exit due to failure in this example. server.close(); return 1; Client example ¶ The client connects to the server at 127.0.0.1:41333 , prints the received events, and sends a notification with the same text. Run the server and client in separate processes. Create the components ¶ The empty manager satisfies the flushAll signature. Sending to the server individually uses the client's connection handle directly. using namespace std::chrono_literals; namespace network = lightnerx::network; namespace communication = lightnerx::communication; network::Client client; network::ConnectionManager connections{0, 0}; // Required by flush, without broadcast. communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; Receive messages from the server ¶ Forward the bytes to authorityInterpret , which interprets messages from the Authority. The callback below prints the text payload agreed upon by these examples and handles empty payloads. client.addServerReceivedMessageCallback([&](std::span bytes) { interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); }); interpreter.addAuthorityInterpretedMessageCallback([](communication::Message message) { const auto text = message.payload.empty() ? std::string_view{} : std::string_view{ reinterpret_cast(message.payload.data()), message.payload.size() }; std::println("Server: {}", text); }); The callbacks use the bytes during the call. To retain a received payload, copy its bytes into application storage before returning. Start and connect ¶ Initialize the client, request a connection to the server, and reserve space in the batcher. The connection will be tracked during calls to update() . if (const auto result = client.start(); !result) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", result.error().message()); return 1; } if (const auto result = client.connect("127.0.0.1", 41333); !result) { std::println("Failed to connect: {}", result.error().message()); return 1; } network::initMessagesBatcher(1); Prepare a notification ¶ Notification uses the total size directly, without bit shifting. ID 47 corresponds to the registration made on the server. const std::string_view greeting = "Hello, World!"; const auto payload = std::as_bytes(std::span{greeting}); const communication::Notification notification{ static_cast(sizeof(communication::Notification) + payload.size()), 47 // The server must register this ID in NotificationRegistry. }; Update and send to the server ¶ Process up to 32 messages per update and send when isConnected() indicates an established connection. Target::single selects the server's handle. while (true) { if (const auto result = client.update(32); !result) { std::println("Failed to update: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (client.isConnected()) { if (const auto result = network::queueMessage(communication::notification2OutboundMessage( notification, payload, network::Target::single(client.getServerHConn()))); !result) { std::println("Failed to queue: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (const auto result = network::flushAll(connections); !result) { std::println("Failed to send: {}", result.error().message()); break; } } std::this_thread::sleep_for(3000ms); } Shut down the client ¶ When exiting due to an error, the Client destructor closes the connection and shuts down the network. Returning 1 indicates the failure that interrupted the example. return 1; // The Client destructor closes the connection and shuts down the network. docs.text: API reference ¶ This page presents the public components grouped by module. All modules are imported with import and belong to the indicated namespaces. Operations that return std::expected<void, std::error_code> can be checked with if (!result) . In the event of an error, result.error() provides the code and result.error().message() provides its description. Complete examples are available in First steps . lightnerx.communication.base_protocol ¶ lightnerx::communication::BaseProtocol ¶ Base structure for headers. BaseProtocol(std::uint16_t size); size : when constructing a message for sending, the encoded size of the Authority's message or the total size of the Obedient's message. The interpreter delivers this field with the size already decoded. Public field: std::uint16_t size . lightnerx.communication.mbt ¶ lightnerx::communication::MBT ¶ Stores the message's semantic identifier. MBT(std::uint16_t type); Public field: std::uint16_t type . Message types ¶ lightnerx.communication.event ¶ lightnerx::communication::Event ¶ Header for an event from the Authority. Event(std::uint16_t size, std::uint16_t typeId); Public fields: protocol : BaseProtocol ; mbt : MBT . lightnerx.communication.notification ¶ lightnerx::communication::Notification ¶ Header for a notification from the Obedient. Notification(std::uint16_t size, std::uint16_t type); Public fields: protocol : BaseProtocol ; mbt : MBT . lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry ¶ Registers IDs that the server should interpret as Notification . void registerId(std::uint16_t id); void registerIds(std::unordered_set<std::uint16_t>&& newIds); bool exist(std::uint16_t id) const noexcept; registerId adds an ID, and registerIds incorporates the IDs from a set passed as a temporary or with std::move . exist() reports whether the ID is registered. The message allocated by the converter is retained, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. If the reserved capacity is occupied, it releases the received message and returns std::errc::not_enough_memory . If message.message is null, it returns std::errc::invalid_argument without queuing. flushAll processes each message separately by sending it to an individual connection, a group, or a broadcast. ConnectionManager is a required argument and provides the broadcast recipients. The function releases all internal messages and empties the queue even when errors occur, returning the last error among the send operations. An empty queue returns success. Calling queueMessage consumes the message, both on success and on error. Pass an existing object with std::move(outbound) or use a converter's result directly. Afterward, do not access, release, or requeue the message. OutboundMessage contains a raw pointer: std::move allows the destination to be moved, but does not automatically set the pointer to null in the original object. Copying the object does not duplicate the message either; therefore, do not pass copies of the same message to the queue. If you never pass a created message to the queue, release it exactly once with Release() . With the network and batcher initialized, and event , payload , connection , and connections defined by the application, typical usage after a converter is: auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::single(connection) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { std::println("Failed to queue: {}", queued.error().message()); } else if (const auto flushed = lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); !flushed) { std::println("Failed to send: {}", flushed.error().message()); } You can also queue multiple messages before calling flushAll . The batcher keeps each message separate, and the application chooses when to flush. Validation and callback behavior ¶ Both interpretation methods accept exactly one complete message. The declared total size must equal the supplied span and include the entire header. Authority sizes are decoded from 15 bits (maximum 32767 bytes); Obedient sizes use 16 bits (maximum 65535 bytes). Truncated headers, mismatched sizes, unknown response status and unregistered Obedient origins produce no callback, matching the existing void parser interface. There is no incremental or concatenated-message framing. Callbacks run synchronously. Registration during a callback is safe; newly registered callbacks participate from the next dispatch, including a nested interpretation. Existing callback objects retain mutable state. Receive/interpreter/ forEach exceptions propagate to their caller, with received buffers released even when a client batch is interrupted. Exceptions from GNS status callbacks are caught at the boundary and the first exception is rethrown by Server::update() after RunCallbacks() returns. A throwing callback ends its current callback sequence. Recursive update() returns operation_in_progress . Callbacks may disconnect or request Server::close() ; do not destroy or assign the component executing a callback. Referenced objects must remain alive until dispatch finishes. A negative receive result returns io_error , distinct from an empty queue; the client also clears and closes its failed connection. Updating an unstarted/closed wrapper returns not_connected . ConnectionManager owns an independent, bidirectional mapping; it neither reads nor writes GNS userdata. A handle may be registered once per manager. Adding a duplicate, invalid handle, or a handle beyond capacity returns nullopt . Different managers may independently register the same valid handle. getClientId() returns nullopt for an absent registration, including handle zero, and retains a registered identity after transport closure until removal. IDs range from 1 to 65535 and are recycled; negative capacities throw invalid_argument , capacity above 65535 is capped. forEach visits the index range present on entry, safely allowing add/remove; it may observe replacements within that range but does not extend traversal for vector growth. The batch queue is global. initMessagesBatcher() reserves capacity without discarding queued messages. clearMessagesBatcher() releases pending messages and preserves capacity; actual network shutdown and queue destruction also release pending messages. flushAll() releases every queued message if a send throws, then propagates the exception; with returned error codes it attempts all entries and returns the last error. Serialize all batch operations, including clearing and shutdown.

docs.text: void initMessagesBatcher(int capacity); void clearMessagesBatcher() noexcept; std::expected<void, std::error_code> queueMessage(OutboundMessage message); std::expected<void, std::error_code> flushAll( const ConnectionManager& connectionManager ); initMessagesBatcher reserves space in the batcher's shared queue. Call it before queuing, with the number of messages you want to be able to keep pending; this reservation does not empty an existing queue. queueMessage receives an OutboundMessage by value and moves it into the queue. The message allocated by the converter is retained, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. If the reserved capacity is occupied, it releases the received message and returns std::errc::not_enough_memory . If message.message is null, it returns std::errc::invalid_argument without queuing. flushAll processes each message separately by sending it to an individual connection, a group, or a broadcast. ConnectionManager is a required argument and provides the broadcast recipients. The function releases all internal messages and empties the queue even when errors occur, returning the last error among the send operations. An empty queue returns success. Calling queueMessage consumes the message, both on success and on error. Pass an existing object with std::move(outbound) or use a converter's result directly. Afterward, do not access, release, or requeue the message. OutboundMessage contains a raw pointer: std::move allows the destination to be moved, but does not automatically set the pointer to null in the original object. Copying the object does not duplicate the message either; therefore, do not pass copies of the same message to the queue. If you never pass a created message to the queue, release it exactly once with Release() . With the network and batcher initialized, and event , payload , connection , and connections defined by the application, typical usage after a converter is: auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::single(connection) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { std::println("Failed to queue: {}", queued.error().message()); } else if (const auto flushed = lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); !flushed) { std::println("Failed to send: {}", flushed.error().message()); } You can also queue multiple messages before calling flushAll . The batcher keeps each message separate, and the application chooses when to flush.

docs.text: Both interpretation methods accept exactly one complete message. The declared total size must equal the supplied span and include the entire header. Authority sizes are decoded from 15 bits (maximum 32767 bytes); Obedient sizes use 16 bits (maximum 65535 bytes). Truncated headers, mismatched sizes, unknown response status and unregistered Obedient origins produce no callback, matching the existing void parser interface. There is no incremental or concatenated-message framing. Callbacks run synchronously. Registration during a callback is safe; newly registered callbacks participate from the next dispatch, including a nested interpretation. Existing callback objects retain mutable state. Receive/interpreter/ forEach exceptions propagate to their caller, with received buffers released even when a client batch is interrupted. Exceptions from GNS status callbacks are caught at the boundary and the first exception is rethrown by Server::update() after RunCallbacks() returns. A throwing callback ends its current callback sequence. Recursive update() returns operation_in_progress . Callbacks may disconnect or request Server::close() ; do not destroy or assign the component executing a callback. Referenced objects must remain alive until dispatch finishes. A negative receive result returns io_error , distinct from an empty queue; the client also clears and closes its failed connection. Updating an unstarted/closed wrapper returns not_connected . ConnectionManager owns an independent, bidirectional mapping; it neither reads nor writes GNS userdata. A handle may be registered once per manager. Adding a duplicate, invalid handle, or a handle beyond capacity returns nullopt . Different managers may independently register the same valid handle. getClientId() returns nullopt for an absent registration, including handle zero, and retains a registered identity after transport closure until removal. IDs range from 1 to 65535 and are recycled; negative capacities throw invalid_argument , capacity above 65535 is capped. forEach visits the index range present on entry, safely allowing add/remove; it may observe replacements within that range but does not extend traversal for vector growth. The batch queue is global. initMessagesBatcher() reserves capacity without discarding queued messages. clearMessagesBatcher() releases pending messages and preserves capacity; actual network shutdown and queue destruction also release pending messages. flushAll() releases every queued message if a send throws, then propagates the exception; with returned error codes it attempts all entries and returns the last error. Serialize all batch operations, including clearing and shutdown.

Interfaces controladas permitem esgotar os 65.535 IDs, devolver alocação nula e provocar erros de recebimento/liberação. Eles não substituem os testes dos módulos reais. O teste de domínio também foi aplicado ao arquivo original de 8e5a352 e falhou em exhausted ID domain must reject add ( build/audit/id-baseline.log ). Reprodução ¶ cmake -S . -B build/audit -G Ninja \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DLIGHTNERX_BUILD_TESTS=ON cmake --build build/audit --parallel 2 ctest --test-dir build/audit --output-on-failure --output-junit test-results.xml -j 2 cmake -S . -B build/audit-sanitizers -G Ninja \ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DLIGHTNERX_BUILD_TESTS=ON \ -DLIGHTNERX_SANITIZERS=address cmake --build build/audit-sanitizers --parallel 2 ctest --test-dir build/audit-sanitizers --output-on-failure --output-junit test-results.xml -j 2 O teste UDP e LeakSanitizer precisam de permissões que o sandbox inicial não oferecia. A execução final usa o ambiente autorizado fora dessa restrição. O limite dos testes que compilam código foi ampliado para 180 segundos após um timeout de compilação concorrente; os limites de runtime permanecem delimitados. Limites dos sanitizadores ¶ Os módulos LightnerX e os consumidores foram compilados com ASan. Os três testes suplementares usam ASan e UBSan, com -fno-sanitize-recover=all , para que qualquer diagnóstico habilitado resulte em falha. A biblioteca padrão e o GNS não foram instrumentados nem tiveram seus fontes alterados. GCC 15.2 aborta com erro interno cp/module.cc:10037 ao compilar estes módulos com UBSan. Isso foi reproduzido tanto instrumentando std quanto deixando std sem instrumentação; portanto não se declara cobertura UBSan dos módulos reais. O GNS vendorizado usa -fno-rtti . Uma reprodução independente, contendo apenas Init/CreatePollGroup/DestroyPollGroup/Kill de GNS, já produz o diagnóstico vptr do UBSan, sem usar LightnerX. O mesmo programa passa quando somente essa checagem é desabilitada ( build/audit/gns-ubsan-probe.cpp e .log ). Por isso apenas o teste suplementar de ciclo de vida, que chama a biblioteca real, usa -fno-sanitize=vptr . Os outros dois testes suplementares não precisam dessa exclusão. Esse diagnóstico foi investigado mesmo quando CTest inicialmente reportou sucesso por causa do modo recuperável padrão do UBSan. API pública e contratos ¶ Client e Server não podem mais ser copiados ou movidos. Server ganha destrutor com limpeza automática; close() é idempotente e noexcept . Apenas um Client ou Server iniciado possui a rede por processo. Start repetido retorna operation_in_progress ; outro owner retorna device_or_resource_busy . networkKill() não invalida um wrapper ativo; o encerramento ocorre quando o owner libera os recursos. Raw GNS Kill/RunCallbacks durante esse ownership não são operações suportadas. disconnect() limpa o estado local imediatamente. Erros de recebimento passam a retornar io_error . Callbacks podem lançar; buffers são liberados e a exceção é propagada. Não se deve destruir o objeto que está despachando um callback. forEach deixa de ser incondicionalmente noexcept . getClientId() consulta pertencimento ao manager e não userdata GNS. A identidade persiste até remoção explícita. O manager deixa userdata para a aplicação. Capacidades negativas são rejeitadas; o domínio é limitado a 65535. Conversores mantêm assinaturas e lançam bad_alloc / length_error em falhas. Mensagens recebidas com tamanho inconsistente são rejeitadas sem callback, conforme a interface de parsing existente, que retorna void . Adicionados clearMessagesBatcher() e Target::isGroup() . A API queueMessage() /Target permanece; mensagens pendentes são liberadas no encerramento e após exceções. initMessagesBatcher() não descarta a fila. Há uma única constante pública k_invalidConnection . CMake propaga C++26 e os requisitos públicos GNS, com setup explícito de import std no consumidor. Não há decisão arquitetural pendente para as correções adotadas. As restrições de múltiplas instâncias, transporte próprio, callbacks e framing foram explicitadas de forma conservadora. A revisão final examinou ownership, ponteiros, liberação parcial de lotes, limites de IDs, reinicialização, composição de módulos e consistência entre código e documentação.

docs.text: Os módulos LightnerX e os consumidores foram compilados com ASan. docs.text: Client e Server não podem mais ser copiados ou movidos. Server ganha destrutor com limpeza automática; close() é idempotente e noexcept . Apenas um Client ou Server iniciado possui a rede por processo. Start repetido retorna operation_in_progress ; outro owner retorna device_or_resource_busy . networkKill() não invalida um wrapper ativo; o encerramento ocorre quando o owner libera os recursos. Raw GNS Kill/RunCallbacks durante esse ownership não são operações suportadas. disconnect() limpa o estado local imediatamente. Erros de recebimento passam a retornar io_error . Callbacks podem lançar; buffers são liberados e a exceção é propagada. Não se deve destruir o objeto que está despachando um callback. forEach deixa de ser incondicionalmente noexcept . getClientId() consulta pertencimento ao manager e não userdata GNS. A identidade persiste até remoção explícita. O manager deixa userdata para a aplicação. Capacidades negativas são rejeitadas; o domínio é limitado a 65535. Conversores mantêm assinaturas e lançam bad_alloc / length_error em falhas. Mensagens recebidas com tamanho inconsistente são rejeitadas sem callback, conforme a interface de parsing existente, que retorna void . Adicionados clearMessagesBatcher() e Target::isGroup() . A API queueMessage() /Target permanece; mensagens pendentes são liberadas no encerramento e após exceções. initMessagesBatcher() não descarta a fila. Há uma única constante pública k_invalidConnection . CMake propaga C++26 e os requisitos públicos GNS, com setup explícito de import std no consumidor. Não há decisão arquitetural pendente para as correções adotadas. As restrições de múltiplas instâncias, transporte próprio, callbacks e framing foram explicitadas de forma conservadora. A revisão final examinou ownership, ponteiros, liberação parcial de lotes, limites de IDs, reinicialização, composição de módulos e consistência entre código e documentação.

docs.text: Communication and the INER protocol ¶ INER and LightnerX ¶ INER is a semantic protocol. It defines the meaning and organization of messages, but does not define sockets, addressing, threads, or the transmission mechanism. LightnerX implements the protocol's message types and provides networking components based on GameNetworkingSockets. The division is: Responsibility INER LightnerX Meaning of Event, Response, Intention, and Notification Yes Represented by C++ types Message identification Yes MBT::type , correlationId , and status fields Header encoding Yes Packed structures and converters Sockets and connections No Server , Client , and GameNetworkingSockets Execution model No Chosen by the application Roles ¶ Authority ¶ The Authority controls internal states. It receives Intention and Notification from the Obedient and sends Event and Response . In LightnerX, the server typically interprets received messages with: interpreter.obedientInterpret(bytes, registry, connection, connections); Obedient ¶ The Obedient sends intentions to the Authority and receives information about occurrences and results. In LightnerX, the client typically interprets received messages with: interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); Message types ¶ Event ¶ Event communicates an occurrence from the Authority. Its header contains: BaseProtocol::size ; MBT::type , used as type_id . The payload, when present, follows the header. Response ¶ Response relates the result to an intention through correlationId and contains a status . The statuses are exposed by constants in the lightnerx.communication.response module: Constant Value Meaning Type used by LightnerX APPROVED_RESPONSE 0 intention fully approved Response DENIED_RESPONSE 1 intention denied UnsuccessfulResponse PARTIALLY_APPROVED_RESPONSE 2 intention partially applied UnsuccessfulResponse FAILURE_RESPONSE 3 internal error during processing Response A failure does not necessarily mean that the intention was denied; the application may decide to try again. UnsuccessfulResponse adds reasonCode to the header of denied or partially approved responses. For partial approval, the meaning of the payload is defined by the application. Intention ¶ Intention requests that the Authority perform an action. Its header contains: BaseProtocol::size ; MBT::type ; correlationId . The intention's payload follows this header. Notification ¶ Notification communicates information to the Authority without requiring state validation, since it does not request a change to the Authority's internal states. Its header contains size and type , followed by the optional payload. On the server, NotificationRegistry specifies which type_id values should be interpreted as Notification : import std; import lightnerx.communication.notification; void registerNotifications(lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry& registry) { registry.registerId(47); registry.registerIds(std::unordered_set<std::uint16_t>{99, 100}); } The type_id values are defined by the application. There is no universal table of INER types. When receiving messages from the Obedient, registered IDs identify notifications; the others identify intentions. To send notifications, use notification2OutboundMessage . Binary representation ¶ Header structures are packed without additional padding using #pragma pack(push, 1) . The converters copy fields in the machine's native representation; participants must use a compatible representation for these fields and agree on the payload format. Messages from the Authority ¶ The first field uses a combined value: the least significant bit indicates whether the message is a Response , and the remaining fifteen bits represent the size. The table describes the recommended formats for emission: approved, denied and failure responses have no payload; partial approval may carry application-defined bytes. Message Header Recommended content when sending Event 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Response 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of correlationId + 1 byte of status no payload for the statuses represented by Response UnsuccessfulResponse Response structure + 2 bytes of reasonCode variable payload for a partial response When constructing the header, the combined value takes the form: Event: (total_size << 1) | 0 Response: (total_size << 1) | 1 The interpreter retrieves the size with base >> 1 and distinguishes Event from Response with base & 1 . In the headers delivered to the callback, protocol.size already contains the decoded size, without the type bit. Reception currently tolerates additional bytes in responses when the declared total matches the supplied span and the selected header is complete. For approved and failure responses, the interpreter ignores those bytes and delivers an empty payload. For denied and partially approved responses, it delivers all bytes after UnsuccessfulResponse , even though the recommended denied-response format has no payload. protocol.size still includes the complete received message, including any ignored bytes; it can therefore exceed the header size plus the delivered payload size. This reception behavior does not change the recommended emission formats. Converters copy the supplied payload without enforcing status-specific payload rules. Messages from the Obedient ¶ In messages from the Obedient, size directly represents the total message size. Message Header Content Notification 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Intention 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type + 2 bytes of correlationId variable payload The specified size must include the header and payload. Each interpretation call must receive exactly one complete message: the decoded total must equal the supplied span and the header must be complete, otherwise no callback is delivered. Authority messages are limited to 32767 bytes and Obedient messages to 65535 bytes. The interpreter does not split concatenated messages or buffer partial frames. Unknown response statuses are ignored. The converters copy the header and payload into a SteamNetworkingMessage_t ; they do not automatically construct the semantic value of the size field. They throw std::bad_alloc if GNS allocation fails and std::length_error if the allocation size cannot be represented. Identifiers ¶ type_id identifies the semantic type defined by the application and appears in the code as MBT::type . correlationId relates a response to its corresponding intention. The ID received in the server's interpreted message callback is the internal identifier assigned by ConnectionManager . This internal ID belongs to the connection management implementation and is not an INER protocol field. The name originId does not designate a protocol field either. Network destinations use HSteamNetConnection handles, which are distinct from internal IDs and semantic identifiers. Network destinations ¶ lightnerx::network::Target , exported by the lightnerx.network.target module, defines where a queued message will be sent. The static factories create the destination description: Factory Destination Target::single(connection) a specific connection Target::group(connections) all connections in the provided vector Target::broadcast() all connections registered in ConnectionManager Target::broadcast(exceptions) all connections registered in ConnectionManager , except the specified handles Target::group stores the explicit selection of handles. Broadcast queries the ConnectionManager passed to flushAll at flush time, using the mappings maintained by the application. Its exceptions are also HSteamNetConnection handles. Receiving flow ¶ Network -> Server callback -> obedientInterpret -> application callback Network -> Client callback -> authorityInterpret -> application callback MessageInterpreter delivers a lightnerx::communication::Message whose header contains the concrete type in a std::variant and whose payload is a std::span<const std::byte> . Callbacks run during the interpretation call. The header is delivered by value, but the span only references the received bytes. In the flow with Server or Client , these bytes are released after the receive callbacks. To retain the payload, copy its bytes during the callback; copying only Message keeps a reference to the same buffer. Sending flow ¶ The usual flow is: Initialize the network and call initMessagesBatcher(capacity) before queuing the first message. Construct the header with the total message size. Create a lightnerx::network::Target . Use the corresponding converter to obtain a lightnerx::network::OutboundMessage . Pass the object to queueMessage(std::move(outbound)) , transferring ownership of the message and destination. Check the queuing result and call flushAll(connectionManager) at the time chosen by the application. Releasing the message becomes the batcher's responsibility, including when queuing returns an error. Example of an Event from the Authority with one byte of payload defined by the application. The function assumes that the network and batcher have been initialized and supports broadcast with or without exceptions: #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" import std; import lightnerx.communication.event; import lightnerx.communication.message; import lightnerx.network.connection_manager; import lightnerx.network.message_batch; import lightnerx.network.target; std::expected<void, std::error_code> broadcastEvent( const lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager& connections, std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> exceptions = {} ) { const std::array payload{std::byte{0x01}}; const auto totalSize = sizeof(lightnerx::communication::Event) + payload.size(); const lightnerx::communication::Event event{ static_cast<std::uint16_t>(totalSize << 1), 47 }; auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::broadcast(std::move(exceptions)) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { return queued; } return lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); } Call broadcastEvent(connections) for everyone or broadcastEvent(connections, {connectionToSkip}) to exclude a handle, checking the returned std::expected . What each step does ¶ queueMessage receives the OutboundMessage from the converter and stores the same message with its destination, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. The call consumes the message: on success, the batcher keeps it until the flush; if the queue is full, it releases it immediately. The caller must not call Release() or reuse the message after passing it to the queue. A null pointer is rejected with invalid_argument . flushAll iterates over pending messages, routes each one according to its destination, and releases the message received from the converter with Release() . All entries are processed and the queue is emptied even when send errors occur. The return value indicates success or the last error encountered among these operations. Batching lets you accumulate multiple messages before a flush. Each entry remains a separate message; payloads are not concatenated. The application decides when to flush, for example at the end of an update. Success indicates that the transport accepted the send operations, without confirming processing by the recipient. For Event and Response , the size field must use the combined value described above. For Intention and Notification , it uses the total size directly. Pending batches can be discarded explicitly with clearMessagesBatcher() and are also released at actual network shutdown. A thrown send exception releases the complete queue before propagating to the caller.

docs.text: First steps ¶ This guide shows the essential flow for setting up a server and a client. The examples use LightnerX components directly and leave the execution model to the application. The two programs illustrate separate consuming applications; the library remains a static library. Server ¶ The server receives bytes from clients, forwards those bytes to MessageInterpreter , and receives interpreted messages through a callback. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" import std; import lightnerx.communication.intention; import lightnerx.communication.message; import lightnerx.communication.notification; import lightnerx.network.connection_manager; import lightnerx.network.server; int main() { lightnerx::network::Server server; lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager connections{10, 10}; lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry registry; registry.registerId(47); server.addClientConnectedCallback( [&connections, &server](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (!connections.add(connection)) { const auto disconnected = server.disconnectConnection(connection, false); if (!disconnected) { std::println("Failed to disconnect: {}", disconnected.error().message()); } } } ); server.addClientDisconnectedCallback( [&connections](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (const auto id = connections.getClientId(connection)) { connections.remove(*id); } } ); server.addClientReceivedMessageCallback( [&interpreter, &registry, &connections]( std::span<const std::byte> bytes, HSteamNetConnection connection ) { interpreter.obedientInterpret( bytes, registry, connection, connections ); } ); interpreter.addObedientInterpretedMessageCallback( [](lightnerx::communication::Message message, std::uint16_t clientId) { std::println("Message received from client {}", clientId); std::visit([](const auto& header) { using Header = std::remove_cvref_t<decltype(header)>; if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Intention>) { std::println("Intention {}, correlation {}", header.mbt.type, header.correlationId); } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Notification>) { std::println("Notification {}", header.mbt.type); } }, message.header); } ); const auto started = server.start(45333, 2500); if (!started) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", started.error().message()); return 1; } while (true) { if (const auto updated = server.update(); !updated) { std::println("Update failed: {}", updated.error().message()); break; } } server.close(); } The connection callback must update the ConnectionManager , because the interpreter uses this object to map the connection to the ID delivered to the interpreted message callback. The lambdas capture the components by reference to connect them. Keep these objects alive as long as their callbacks may run. The received payload points to the network message's bytes; copy the bytes during the callback if you need to use them later. Client ¶ The client forwards bytes received from the server to the authorityInterpret method. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" import std; import lightnerx.communication.event; import lightnerx.communication.message; import lightnerx.communication.response; import lightnerx.network.client; int main() { lightnerx::network::Client client; lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; client.addServerReceivedMessageCallback( [&interpreter](std::span<const std::byte> bytes) { interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); } ); interpreter.addAuthorityInterpretedMessageCallback( [](lightnerx::communication::Message message) { std::visit([](const auto& header) { using Header = std::remove_cvref_t<decltype(header)>; if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Event>) { std::println("Event {}", header.mbt.type); } else if constexpr ( std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Response> || std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::UnsuccessfulResponse> ) { std::println("Response to intention {}: status {}", header.correlationId, header.status); if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::UnsuccessfulResponse>) { std::println("Reason {}", header.reasonCode); } } }, message.header); } ); if (const auto started = client.start(); !started) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", started.error().message()); return 1; } if (const auto connected = client.connect("127.0.0.1", 45333); !connected) { std::println("Failed to connect: {}", connected.error().message()); return 1; } while (true) { if (const auto updated = client.update(1); !updated) { std::println("Update failed: {}", updated.error().message()); break; } } } connect() initiates the connection, and update() processes network callbacks and available messages. isConnected() can be used to query the state observed by the client. Execution model ¶ The server.update() and client.update() methods are called by the application. They can run on the main thread, on a dedicated thread, or within the consuming project's existing execution loop. The library does not require a specific number of threads or a fixed interval between updates. Run these server and client examples in separate processes: exactly one started wrapper owns networking in each process. Wrappers cannot be copied or moved. Receive callbacks run during update() , and interpretation callbacks run on the thread that calls the interpreter. When sharing components across threads, handle synchronization in the application. For the batcher, serialize initialization, queuing, clearing and flush calls, which operate on the same queue. Callback exceptions propagate after resource cleanup; catch them around update() if the application intends to continue. See callback behavior for supported reentrant operations. Batch sending ¶ With the network initialized by Server::start() , Client::start() , or lightnerx::network::networkInit() , reserve space in the batcher before queuing the first message. Import lightnerx.network.message_batch and call: lightnerx::network::initMessagesBatcher(64); The destination is defined by lightnerx::network::Target . The following function creates an Event , routes it to a group, and sends the queue. It assumes the initialization above and returns the result of queuing or flushing to the caller. docs.text: The server.update() and client.update() methods are called by the application. They can run on the main thread, on a dedicated thread, or within the consuming project's existing execution loop. The library does not require a specific number of threads or a fixed interval between updates. Run these server and client examples in separate processes: exactly one started wrapper owns networking in each process. Wrappers cannot be copied or moved. Receive callbacks run during update() , and interpretation callbacks run on the thread that calls the interpreter. When sharing components across threads, handle synchronization in the application. For the batcher, serialize initialization, queuing, clearing and flush calls, which operate on the same queue. Callback exceptions propagate after resource cleanup; catch them around update() if the application intends to continue. See callback behavior for supported reentrant operations.

docs.text: Setup ¶ LightnerX is a static C++ library. The project provides the LightnerX target and does not have its own executable. GameNetworkingSockets ¶ GameNetworkingSockets is maintained as a submodule in external/GameNetworkingSockets . After obtaining the repository, run the following from the LightnerX root directory: git submodule update --init --recursive This command retrieves GameNetworkingSockets and its recursive submodules in the state expected by LightnerX. Toolchain and build ¶ LightnerX uses C++26 named modules and import std . The verified Linux toolchain is GCC 15.2 with its matching libstdc++, CMake 4.2.3 and Ninja 1.13.2. Install the GameNetworkingSockets prerequisites (including OpenSSL and Protobuf development packages and the Protobuf compiler) before configuring. Compilers and standard libraries without a C++26 std module are not supported by this configuration. cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug cmake --build build --parallel 2 Consuming with CMake ¶ The LightnerX target propagates C++26, GameNetworkingSockets headers, compile definitions and link requirements. Consumers should link only that target. CMake's experimental import std support must be enabled before the parent project's first project() call . This gate is specific to CMake 4.2; consult the installed CMake documentation before changing CMake versions. cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 4.2) set(CMAKE_EXPERIMENTAL_CXX_IMPORT_STD "d0edc3af-4c50-42ea-a356-e2862fe7a444") set(CMAKE_CXX_MODULE_STD ON) set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF) project(MyGame LANGUAGES C CXX) add_subdirectory(external/LightnerX) add_executable(game main.cpp) target_link_libraries(game PRIVATE LightnerX) #include <steam/steamnetworkingsockets.h> import std; import lightnerx.network.client; int main() { lightnerx::network::Client client; return client.start() ? 0 : 1; } No prebuilt module binaries are distributed: the consumer and library must use compatible compiler, standard-library and module settings. The standalone tests/consumer project verifies this integration, including simultaneous imports of the client and transport modules. Regression tests and sanitizers ¶ The regression suite also requires Python 3 for deterministic fault-injection tests that compile the production implementation with a small transport mock. cmake -S . -B build/tests -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DLIGHTNERX_BUILD_TESTS=ON cmake --build build/tests --parallel 2 ctest --test-dir build/tests --output-on-failure With the tested GCC 15.2 toolchain, instrument the modules with AddressSanitizer: cmake -S . -B build/sanitizers -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \ -DLIGHTNERX_BUILD_TESTS=ON -DLIGHTNERX_SANITIZERS=address cmake --build build/sanitizers --parallel 2 ctest --test-dir build/sanitizers --output-on-failure This option instruments LightnerX and its consumers, including the tests; it does not instrument the standard-library module or third-party libraries. On a compatible compiler, -DLIGHTNERX_SANITIZERS=address,undefined enables both ASan and UBSan. GCC 15.2 hits an internal compiler error when compiling these modules with UBSan, even if std itself is not instrumented. The supplemental Python fault tests compile the production bodies without module declarations and run both sanitizers whenever LIGHTNERX_SANITIZERS is enabled; they supplement the real module tests rather than replacing them. Sanitizer diagnostics fail the test immediately. The lifecycle fault test links the real GNS library, which is built with -fno-rtti ; only that supplemental test disables UBSan's vptr check. A raw GNS init/CreatePollGroup/Kill probe reproduces the incompatible check without using LightnerX. ASan and the other UBSan checks remain enabled. The allocation and ID mocks do not need this exclusion. Network integration tests require local UDP socket access. Restricted sandboxes may prevent those tests from completing; a build alone does not validate network behavior. Test assertions remain enabled in release configurations.
